summary_paragraph: A man with non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy, COPD, and a history of cocaine dependence was admitted for acute respiratory distress and hypoxia. He presented with progressive shortness of breath, cough with yellowish sputum, and diffuse chest tightness, despite denying recent crack use. Initial evaluation revealed bilateral lung opacities on imaging, elevated BNP, and leukocytosis. He was treated for both acute on chronic systolic heart failure and crack cocaine pneumonitis. Aggressive diuresis was initiated but provided limited respiratory improvement, leading to a diagnosis of predominant pneumonitis. He was started on steroids and antibiotics, with gradual improvement in oxygenation and lung findings. His diabetes was managed with increased insulin due to steroid use, later tapered back. He was transitioned from metoprolol to carvedilol, and lisinopril was reduced. He was discharged home after eight days, ambulating independently on room air, with a plan for outpatient follow-up and nicotine replacement therapy.
problems: Bronchitis and pneumonitis due to fumes and vapors
